examples.title: Push buttons and default action
examples.states: Normal, pressed, focused, disabled, and default action. The default outline is separate from keyboard focus.
examples.keys: Tab moves focus; Space activates a focused button. Enter in the name field submits the form.
examples.note: A default action must be safe in context. Browser form submission supplies Enter behavior; this is not a global Enter shortcut.

examples.title: Toggle buttons
examples.states: Off/on, pressed feedback, focus, and disabled on state.
examples.keys: Space or Enter toggles the focused button.
examples.note: Keep the label stable and expose its persistent state with aria-pressed. A momentary command needs no aria-pressed.

examples.title: Checkboxes and mixed state
examples.states: Unchecked, checked, mixed aggregate, focused, disabled checked.
examples.keys: Tab visits each enabled checkbox; Space toggles. Activating a mixed parent selects all children.
examples.note: Mixed describes an aggregate, not a third saved boolean. Setting indeterminate is separate from checked.

examples.title: Radio-button groups
examples.states: One selected option, focus, and disabled option. The legend labels the choice as a whole.
examples.keys: Tab enters or leaves the group; arrow keys choose among enabled options; Space selects.
examples.note: Native inputs with a shared name supply mutual exclusion and keyboard behavior. Separate unrelated groups need different names.

examples.title: Text fields and validation
examples.states: Editable, read-only (selectable), disabled, password, and invalid with a connected explanation.
examples.keys: Native selection, clipboard, Home/End and text editing keys remain available. Enter submits.
examples.note: Do not intercept typing to implement application shortcuts. Validation appears beside the field and uses browser constraint validation.

examples.title: Multiline text
examples.states: Multiple lines, selection, scrolling, focus and resize.
examples.keys: Enter inserts a new line; Tab moves to Save. Native Ctrl+A/C/X/V and navigation work.
examples.note: This is plain text. RichEdit, embedded objects and document formatting need a separate editor integration.

examples.title: Numeric field and spin control
examples.states: Editable, increment/decrement, minimum/maximum and invalid typed values.
examples.keys: Up/Down changes one step; typing and native text selection work. Tab exits.
examples.note: A native number input avoids inventing text editing rules. Its arrow artwork is browser dependent; paired custom spin buttons must preserve the same labeled field and bounds.

examples.title: Drop-down selection
examples.states: Closed/open, selected option, disabled option and disabled control.
examples.keys: Native arrows, type-ahead, Alt+Down and Escape behavior follow the browser and host.
examples.note: The popup belongs to the browser or OS. Do not promise pixel-identical option menus on every host.

examples.title: Editable combo box
examples.states: Free text, filtered suggestions, active suggestion distinct from committed value, empty results, closed popup.
examples.keys: Down/Up opens and moves suggestions; Enter accepts; Escape dismisses without replacing text; Tab leaves. Home/End edit text.
examples.note: A modern ARIA adaptation. DOM focus stays in the field while aria-activedescendant names the current option. Native edit keys are not captured.

examples.title: Single-selection list box
examples.states: Selected row, focus, scroll and disabled item. Selection does not activate the document.
examples.keys: Arrows, Home/End and type-ahead choose an item; Tab reaches Open; Enter activates the button.
examples.note: This native list deliberately keeps selection and the explicit Open action separate.

examples.title: Multiple-selection list box
examples.states: Discontiguous selections, range selection and empty selection.
examples.keys: Native modifier+arrow/Space selection varies by platform; Ctrl+A selects all on Windows. Tab leaves.
examples.note: The native multiple select retains host keyboard behavior; custom lists must choose and document a selection model.

examples.title: Group boxes and labels
examples.states: Etched group, legend interrupting the border, labels, enabled and disabled groups.
examples.keys: The group itself adds no Tab stop. Tab and arrows operate the contained controls.
examples.note: Use fieldset and legend for a related set. Borders alone do not provide the group name to assistive technology.

examples.title: Horizontal and vertical sliders
examples.states: Horizontal/vertical, value, bounds, focus and disabled.
examples.keys: Native arrows change a step; Home/End reach bounds. The vertical slider uses Up to increase.
examples.note: CSS writing-mode is a modern browser adaptation; verify orientation and keys in each browser you support.

examples.title: Progress bars
examples.states: Determinate, indeterminate, complete and canceled.
examples.keys: The bar is not a Tab stop. Buttons operate this manually advanced demonstration.
examples.note: Use a real job’s measurements in an app; do not invent percentages. Announce milestones instead of every animation frame.

examples.title: Scrollbars and scrolling regions
examples.states: Two axes, thumb, track, focus and resizable viewport.
examples.keys: Focus the region; arrows/Page Up/Page Down scroll. Wheel and touch retain native behavior.
examples.note: WebKit scrollbar styling is approximate and platform dependent. Arrow glyphs and always-visible bars are not guaranteed; use native overflow before implementing a custom scrollbar.

examples.title: Tooltips and status help
examples.states: Delayed hover/focus hint, Escape dismissal, supplemental status text.
examples.keys: Tab focuses the command; Escape dismisses its tooltip; Enter or Space runs it.
examples.note: The button has a meaningful visible label without a tooltip. Essential instructions must remain visible. This noninteractive tooltip uses aria-describedby.

examples.title: Tabs and tab panels
examples.states: Selected tab, inactive tabs, focus, persistent values in hidden panels.
examples.keys: Tab enters the active tab; Left/Right and Home/End select tabs; Tab enters the active panel.
examples.note: Automatic activation is appropriate for these local, instant panels. Later guidance discourages multiple rows; use a layout that keeps labels readable.

examples.title: Toolbar buttons and groups
examples.states: Commands, toggles, separator, disabled command and one Tab stop.
examples.keys: Tab enters/leaves; Left/Right and Home/End move within the toolbar; Space/Enter activates.
examples.note: Text labels make this sample self-contained. Icon-only versions need accessible names and visible tooltip/status help.

examples.title: Tree view
examples.states: Expanded/collapsed branches, visible focus and single selection; children retain their state when a parent closes.
examples.keys: Up/Down visits visible rows; Right expands or enters a branch; Left collapses or reaches its parent; Home/End and type-ahead navigate; Enter opens.
examples.note: This tree chooses selection-follows-focus. Multiselect trees and drag-and-drop are separate interaction models, not implied by this sample.

examples.title: List view and sortable columns
examples.states: Details/icons, selected item, focus and ascending/descending sort; selection survives reordering.
examples.keys: Tab visits sort buttons and the selected row; arrows and Home/End change row; Enter opens. Header buttons sort.
examples.note: A compact single-selection file list, not an editable spreadsheet grid. The responsive icon view uses linear arrow navigation. Use a full grid model for editable cells.

examples.title: Column header and resizing
examples.states: Sort direction, bounded width, pointer resizing, focus and keyboard resizing.
examples.keys: Focus the separator; Left/Right changes width 5%; Home/End reaches bounds; Escape cancels an active pointer drag.
examples.note: The column divider uses the modern separator pattern and exposes its width. Sorting remains a separate button.

examples.title: Resizable split panes
examples.states: Bounded pane widths, pointer capture, keyboard focus and canceled drag.
examples.keys: Tab reaches the divider; Left/Right adjusts 5%; Home/End reaches limits; Escape cancels an active drag.
examples.note: The divider is not a scroll bar. Touch resizing uses pointer events; minimum widths keep both panes reachable.

examples.title: Menu bar, submenus and recent files
examples.states: Menu-bar mode, dropdown, delayed pointer submenu, disabled item, check mark, exclusive radio mark and numbered inline MRU group.
examples.keys: Alt alone or F10 focuses the bar; Alt+F/V opens a menu. Arrows navigate; Enter/Space activates; underlined letters select. Escape closes one layer at a time, then exits the bar and restores focus. Tab leaves.
examples.note: The 1995 draft describes staged menu dismissal and sparse cascades. Short inline MRUs above a separated final Exit match period examples; long/grouped histories may use a submenu. ARIA and the 350 ms pointer delay are explicit browser choices. Ctrl+N is illustrative menu text, not a registered browser shortcut.

examples.title: Context menus
examples.states: Pointer and keyboard invocation, disabled command, bounded horizontal placement and focus restoration.
examples.keys: Shift+F10 or the context-menu key opens for the focused document; Up/Down, Home/End and mnemonic letters navigate; Enter selects; Escape restores focus.
examples.note: A context menu supplements visible commands in a real app. This sample uses no menu bar; browser context menus outside its target remain available.

examples.title: Modal dialog and focus restoration
examples.states: Closed/open modal, default action, validation, cancellation, inert background and restored focus.
examples.keys: Tab stays within the native dialog; Enter submits the field; Escape cancels; closing returns focus to Rename document.
examples.note: Native HTML dialog supplies browser modality. Electron caption buttons and other native host windows require separate coordination; CSS cannot block host window controls.

examples.title: Modeless Find dialog
examples.states: Open without blocking the document, repeated search, wraparound, match-case and not found.
examples.keys: Tab can leave the dialog for the document. Enter runs Find next; Escape closes when focus is in the dialog; Close restores its trigger.
examples.note: HTML dialog.show() is modeless. This example stays in document flow rather than pretending to manage native desktop window stacking.

examples.title: Property sheet with Apply and Cancel
examples.states: Cross-page draft, Apply enabled only when changed, OK commit/close, Cancel rollback since last Apply, explicit caption Close decision.
examples.keys: Arrows switch tabs; Tab enters fields; Escape inside the sheet acts as Cancel. Caption Close offers Apply, Discard, or Keep editing when dirty.
examples.note: A fixed-object modeless property sheet. Apply commits every page and Cancel never undoes an earlier Apply. The draft’s distinct Close behavior is modeled explicitly here; it is not a requirement to prompt on every dialog’s X.

examples.title: Message box and safe default
examples.states: Question, destructive action, safe initial focus/default and explicit outcome.
examples.keys: Enter initially cancels; Tab reaches Delete; Escape cancels; focus returns to the trigger.
examples.note: Action labels say what will happen. A destructive choice should not become the initial default merely because it is visually primary. Nothing on disk is removed.

examples.title: Wizard with validation and backtracking
examples.states: First/middle/final step, required input, preserved draft while going Back, Finish commit and Cancel discard.
examples.keys: Tab operates the current page. Back/Next are explicit buttons; Escape cancels. Step heading receives focus when the page changes.
examples.note: This is an original small workflow, not a generic wizard framework. Page transitions validate only the information needed to proceed.

examples.title: Palette, color well and color dialog
examples.states: Swatches, RGB values, preview draft, committed well, validation and cancel rollback.
examples.keys: Tab reaches the palette and numeric fields; arrows select a palette color; native number arrows edit components; Escape cancels.
examples.note: A deliberately small browser color dialog. It does not emulate the native Windows custom-color store, hue/saturation plane, system palette or color management.

examples.title: Font dialog with sample
examples.states: Family, size, bold/italic, live draft sample, commit and cancel.
examples.keys: Native select, numeric and checkbox keys work; Escape cancels; focus returns to Choose font.
examples.note: Browser CSS requests fonts; fallback depends on installed fonts. This is not native font enumeration or a RichEdit formatting engine.

examples.title: Window shell, system menu, move and size
examples.states: Active caption, system menu, normal/minimized/maximized/restored bounds, close/reopen, move/size and cancellation.
examples.keys: Alt+Space within the sample opens its system menu. Choose Move or Size, then arrows (Shift for 1 px), Enter to keep, Escape to revert. Caption buttons are labeled.
examples.note: A browser child-window pattern, not OS window chrome or full MDI management. Native Electron controls must use host APIs. This sample constrains geometry to its workspace.

examples.title: Open file through the browser
examples.states: No selection, chosen file, successful read, preview limit and read failure. Canceling the host picker keeps the existing document.
examples.keys: Tab reaches the native file input; activate it to open the host picker. Picker navigation and cancellation belong to the browser/OS.
examples.note: A working host adapter, not a drawn Windows 95 file dialog. A browser cannot enumerate arbitrary folders or guarantee native MRU/filter behavior. Only a user-selected file is read.

examples.title: Save file through the browser
examples.states: Edited content/name and a real UTF-8 text download request.
examples.keys: Tab reaches Save; Space or Enter requests the download. Destination prompts follow browser settings.
examples.note: The browser may download immediately or ask for a destination. A download request is not proof a file was saved. For overwrite confirmation, persistent paths and native Save As, use a host adapter.

examples.title: Print through the browser
examples.states: Screen/print layouts and print-dialog lifecycle.
examples.keys: Activate Print to use the host dialog; its controls and Escape behavior are native.
examples.note: Page Setup, Print Setup, printer capabilities and actual job completion need host integration. afterprint also fires when printing is canceled.

examples.title: Hot-key input
examples.states: Recorded chord, empty value, canceled capture and invalid chord.
examples.keys: Modified keys record a shortcut; Tab always leaves; Escape reverts to the value at focus entry.
examples.note: A browser capture field, not the Windows hot-key common control. Reserved OS/browser chords may never reach the page. A consuming app must validate conflicts and registration failures.

examples.title: Rich text editing boundary
examples.states: Editable rich content, selection, multiline input, browser clipboard and undo.
examples.keys: Native contenteditable editing keys apply. Tab leaves the editor; the example registers no formatting shortcuts.
examples.note: This is a browser adapter with basic editing only, not a reusable RichEdit/RTF engine. Production formatting, reliable undo, safe paste/import and serialization need a dedicated editor or native RichEdit. Never insert untrusted HTML directly.

examples.title: Animation display
examples.states: Static initial image, explicit play/stop and accessible description.
examples.keys: Tab reaches Play; Space/Enter toggles playback.
examples.note: Original SVG artwork and Web Animations replace the period AVI animation control. Motion never auto-starts; this sample carries no AVI decoding or native common-control implementation.
